Note · Doerr — Measure What Matters

3 min read722 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-doerr-measure-what-matters.md

Canon · Cluster: Org Design & Mechanisms · Maps to Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making), Course 09 (Leadership & OB)

  • Source: John Doerr, Measure What Matters (2018) — the OKR system, inherited from Grove at Intel
  • Core claim: OKRs create alignment, focus, and accountability — but only if treated as a direction-setting tool, not a task list.
  • Framework:
  • Objective — what you want to achieve: qualitative, inspiring, slightly uncomfortable.
  • Key Results — how you'll know you got there: quantitative, specific, time-bound (3–5 per O).
  • Properties: alignment (everyone sees how their work connects up), focus (few objectives per cycle), accountability (results tracked publicly).
  • Calibration: ~70% achievement is the sweet spot — hitting 100% means you sandbagged. (Stretch OKRs vs. committed OKRs are scored differently.)
  • Applies when: an org is busy but unaligned — OKRs force the conversation about the few things that matter and make progress visible.
  • Breaks when: the #1 failure mode is treating OKRs as a to-do list — bottom-up activity dressed as outcomes. They also corrupt when tied to compensation (people sandbag to hit bonuses, killing the stretch). KR-gaming: people optimize the metric, not the goal (Goodhart's law). And cascading OKRs rigidly top-down recreates the leader-follower trap that canon marquet turn the ship around warns against — Doerr advocates a mix of top-down and bottom-up.
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/ExperiencedDevs corpus + Lenny's Podcast / Will Larson transcript) Goodhart's law isn't a footnote in the wild — it's the dominant complaint. In r/ExperiencedDevs "I'm giving up; Becoming a yes man" (1,668↑) a senior engineer lists what actually gets rewarded: "Ability to attach metrics to your work and then make those metrics look good… It doesn't matter if you have high quality & actionable metrics, you just need numbers that look good. '200% increase in usage' sounds better than 'we have 2 new users.'" That is the KR-gaming failure mode the book warns about, observed live. But the deeper corpus critique is Larson's: teams confuse measuring progress with making it — "we weren't actually prioritizing improvements, we were just prioritizing measurement" (Lenny's Podcast). The Grove original (canon grove high output management) was leaner precisely because it kept the metric subordinate to the outcome.
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): The point of an objective-and-metric system is focus through constraint, not coverage. Larson frames it the way Doerr frames a good Objective: "the goal of good strategy is not to appease everyone… the goal of good strategy is to dictate how we invest the limited capacities we have into the problems we care about" (Lenny's Podcast — Will Larson). OKRs are that constraint made legible: a few objectives, public, that "focus people's energy on the problems that we value as a company."
  • Real application (mined): The corpus surfaces the right unit of measurement — outcomes, not activity. A r/ExperiencedDevs thread, "A 5 min weekly habit completely changed my performance review" (1,611↑), describes a weekly "brag document" logging top accomplishments; it works because it tracks results shipped, not hours worked — the same O-vs-task-list distinction Doerr insists on, applied to one engineer's quarter.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: Practitioners report that once a number is the target, people optimize the number, not the goal — "you just need numbers that look good" (r/ExperiencedDevs, 1,668↑) — and that measurement itself can crowd out the work: "we weren't actually prioritizing improvements, we were just prioritizing measurement… you do have to cut at some point to actually make impact" (Larson). The KR is a proxy; the corpus reality is that proxies get gamed and rituals calcify unless leadership keeps re-anchoring on the real Objective.
  • Sources in corpus: Lenny's Podcast — "The engineering mindset | Will Larson (Carta, Stripe, Uber, Calm, Digg)" (youtube.com/watch?v=Z9ftpRhRiJE) · r/ExperiencedDevs "I'm giving up; Becoming a yes man" (1,668↑), "A 5 min weekly habit changed my performance review" (1,611↑).

Rep

Write one Objective + 3 Key Results for your own quarter. Test it: is the O a direction (could fail) or a disguised task list? Are the KRs numbers, not activities?
